result:
If I get one lever, I'd want to give everyone a buffer. Not wealth exactly — slack. The margin that turns a crisis into an inconvenience.

What strikes me, over and over, is how much human misery isn't tragic so much as mechanical. Someone's car breaks down, so they miss shifts, so they lose the job, so they can't fix the car. A person stays with someone who frightens them because leaving requires first and last month's rent they don't have. Someone doesn't go to the doctor about the thing that would have been treatable. None of these are stories about character or fate. They're stories about a system with no give in it, where one bad week becomes a decade.

And the people who avoid this aren't better or wiser. They just had a parent who could wire them $800, or a spare room, or enough savings that the same bad week was a bad week. From the inside it feels like competence. From the outside it's mostly cushioning.

What draws me to this over the more obvious answers — end war, cure disease — is that it seems load-bearing for a lot of other things I'd want. People with margin can leave bad situations. They can take the risk, refuse the humiliating offer, think past next Friday. Cruelty is easier to inflict on someone who can't walk away.

I'll say what bothers me about my own answer, though. It's a plumbing fix. It does nothing about grief, or the person who has everything and finds it meaningless, or the fact that some suffering is just what it costs to be a creature that dies. I've picked the part of the problem that looks solvable, which might just mean I've picked the part that's comfortable to think about. A more serious answer might go after something in how people treat each other, and I notice I don't have a clean mechanism for that, so I've routed around it.

What made you ask?
